title: Act four, the landing, and a stranger on a call
summary: Write and perform the hardest act of the Talk, the one about the season you are still standing inside, build the thirty seconds it lands on, then run the whole thing cold past somebody who was not here and repair the first hole they find while they are still on the call.
materials: the Expedition dossier, open at the Talk pages
the drafts of acts one, two and three, and whatever you wrote about the seeds
the dawn log, the pace pages, the Bestiary and the bug diary, all out on the table
a timer, for the acts and for nothing else
a grandparent or another adult on a call who has not been told the story

steps.title: Telling a story you are standing inside
steps.body:
Three acts of the Talk exist. The forest, the coast, the mountains, all drafted at oases, all performed once with something in your hands. Today you write the fourth, and the fourth is different from the other three in a way that is worth naming before you start.

Acts one, two and three were about seasons that had finished. A finished season has already sorted itself out: you know which parts mattered, which disaster turned out to be funny, and where it ended. Act four is about the season you are standing inside right now. Nothing has sorted itself out. You do not yet know which part of this summer will turn out to have been the important one, and you are going to have to say something about it anyway, on a stage, to people who were not there.

That is the craft problem of the week, and it is also this week's question. When you tell the story of this season you will leave things out. You have to; ten minutes is ten minutes and this summer is not ten minutes long. You will choose an order that makes one thing lead to another, even where they only happened to be next to each other. You will make the thing you decided at the end sound like something you were heading towards from the start, because that is what a shape does. None of that is inventing anything. All of it is choosing.

So: what makes a story true, the facts or the shape you give them? A talk with every fact in it and no shape is not true, it is just long. A talk with a beautiful shape and one fact bent to fit is a lie with good posture. Somewhere between those there is an honest talk, and finding it is the actual job today.

Two more things get built this hour after act four. The landing, because a talk's last thirty seconds are the part a room carries out of the door, and yours has a particular thing to land on. And then the stranger test, which is the only reliable way to find out whether any of this works, because everybody in this house already knows the story and cannot hear it any more.

steps.title: Act four, the desert
steps.body:
Act four, the desert. About under three minutes, same length as the others.

The rule that has run since act one still runs: say what changed, not what happened. A list of what happened is a diary. An act is what you could not do at the start and can do now.

But this act needs a different way in, because you cannot look back at this season from outside it. So build it from evidence instead of from memory, and you happen to have unusual amounts of evidence lying around: the dawn log, the pace pages, the Bestiary, the bug diary, the dossier, and a folder full of programs in two languages. Go and look at them before you write a word. Reading your own week 1 Bestiary entries is the fastest way to find out how far you have come, and it is more honest than trying to remember.

Then choose three moments. Not five, not the whole summer. Three. One where something was hard in a way you did not expect. One where something turned out to be easier than it looked, because a talk that is all struggle is a boasting talk wearing a humble coat. And one that you cannot fully explain yet, which you say out loud as something you cannot fully explain yet. That third one is what makes act four honest rather than tidy, and it is the thing acts one to three could not have.

Then the seeds. Act one planted something. You either paid a little of it off in acts two and three or you planted a second thing, and the dossier says which. Act four is where the harvest happens. Go and read what you actually wrote down rather than trusting yourself to remember it, and write in the margin exactly which line of act four pays off which line of act one.

Perform it once, timed, and write the time down. Then mark two lines to cut. Choosing what to leave out is a skill of its own, and it is the skill this week is about.
checklist: I read the dawn log, the pace pages and my own week 1 Bestiary entries before writing a word of act four
The act is built on three chosen moments, one of them a thing I said out loud that I cannot fully explain yet
I read back what the dossier says about the seeds, and wrote in the margin which line of act four pays off which line of act one
The act was performed once, timed, and the time is written in the dossier
Two lines are marked for cutting

steps.title: The landing
steps.body:
Now the landing, which is the last thirty seconds and is not the same job as the last act.

Here is the shape the Talk has. Four acts, one per season, and then it lands on something you hold up: the Autumn Protocol, your plan for your own hours after this season ends, in your handwriting. That page does not exist yet and it does not need to today. What you build today is what you say while you are holding it, and the shape of the ending is what makes the page mean something when it finally appears.

Three things a landing has to do, and it has about thirty seconds to do all three.

It has to answer the question the talk has been asking. That question is yours: you decided what these four seasons were about, and it is written in the dossier. Read what you wrote and make sure the landing actually answers it rather than changing the subject to something easier to say.

It has to be about what happens next rather than about what happened. The four acts are the past. The landing is the only part that faces the other way, and a talk that ends by summarising itself has ended twice.

And it has to be short enough to say without notes while holding something in one hand. Write it, then say it standing up with an object in your hand and see which words you drop. The words you drop under those conditions were decoration.

One thing to decide out loud and write in the dossier: does the landing end on you, or on the room? Both are real endings. Ending on you says here is what I am going to do. Ending on the room says here is what I am asking you for, and yours has a job printed on it for two other people. Pick one on purpose, because a landing that tries to do both does neither.

The Talk's opening is not settled today. That gets fixed later, with the running order. Endings are harder than openings and they go first.
checklist: The landing answers the question I decided these four seasons were about, and I checked it against what the dossier actually says
It faces forwards rather than summarising the acts behind it
I said it standing up with something in one hand, and cut the words I dropped
I decided out loud whether it ends on me or on the room, and wrote which in the dossier

steps.title: The stranger test
steps.body:
The stranger test, and it is the only honest measurement in this hour.

Everybody in this house has watched this summer happen. They cannot hear your talk any more; they hear their own memories with your voice over the top. So the talk has to meet somebody who was not here. A grandparent on a call is ideal, and anybody counts as long as they are fond of you, genuinely have not been told the story, and can be trusted to say a true thing.

The setup, and each part of it matters.

Tell them what the test is before you start, in one sentence: I am going to talk for a while, and your job is to tell me the places where you got lost. Say plainly that lost is the useful answer and lovely is not.

Then perform it cold. What you have of it, in order, no stopping to explain, no side remarks to the camera, no it will make sense in a minute. The moment you explain something out loud you have hidden the exact hole you were trying to find.

Give them something to do with their hands. Ask them to say the word what, out loud, the instant they lose the thread, and to keep it to that one word. Long polite feedback afterwards is nearly useless because people forget where they stopped following. A what lands on the sentence.

Then ask them three questions and write the answers down word for word without arguing with any of them. What is this talk about, in one sentence? Which part was longest? Which part would you tell somebody else about?

The last of those three is the important one. What a stranger repeats to somebody else is what your talk actually is, whatever you intended it to be.

Then fix one thing, on the spot, while they are still on the call. One. Take the first place they said what and repair it right there, out loud, and perform that piece again to the same person. Repairing it later from notes is how a note becomes a plan and a plan becomes nothing.

And listen properly to what a stalling point actually is. When somebody gets lost it is almost never that they are slow. It is that you used a word you own and they do not, or you skipped a step you take a thousand times a day, or you left out who somebody is. Those are the same three holes that make a program wrong, and you know how to look for them.
checklist: The stranger was told that lost is the useful answer, before anything was performed
I performed it cold, in order, and explained nothing out loud while it was running
They said what at every place they lost the thread, and I wrote down where
Their three answers are written word for word, including the one about what they would tell somebody else
I repaired the first stalling point on the spot and performed that piece again to the same person

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record act four and the landing, performed back to back with whatever you will be holding up at the end, or a stand-in for it. Then keep rolling for two more things. First, read out the stranger's three answers exactly as you wrote them down, including the one you liked least. Then answer this week's question straight to camera: what makes a story true, the facts or the shape you give them, and what is your reason?
